title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
notes: **Electric current.** Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = q/t; its SI unit is the ampere (1 A = 1 C/s) and conventional current is taken from positive to negative.
**Drift velocity.** Free electrons gain a tiny average velocity v_d along the field between collisions: v_d = eEτ/m = eVτ/(ml); it is of the order of mm/s even in strong currents.
**Relation I = nAev_d.** In time t electrons move v_d·t, so the charge crossing area A is q = nAev_d·t, giving I = nAev_d, where n is the number of free electrons per unit volume.
**Current density and mobility.** J = I/A = nev_d is the current density; mobility μ = v_d/E, and conductivity σ = neμ connects drift to the microscopic picture.
**Macroscopic vs microscopic.** Ohm's law in microscopic form is J = σE; the same field that drives the drift also sustains the current the ammeter reads.

A current of one ampere in a typical metal wire needs only a tiny drift speed, often a fraction of a millimetre per second. The lamp still lights at once because the electric field, not the drifting electron, carries the signal along the wire.

**Current and drift quantities (classified)**

| Quantity | Symbol/Formula | Unit | Typical size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Current | I = Q/t = neAv_d | A | 1 A in a wire |
| Drift velocity | v_d = I/(neA) | m/s | fraction of a mm/s |
| Number density | n | m⁻³ | ≈10²⁸ for copper |
| Current density | J = I/A | A/m² | — |

**Why the lamp lights instantly though v_d is tiny**

| Step | Explanation | Exam line |
|---|---|---|
| Field travels fast | EM field propagates near light speed | The push is instant |
| All electrons drift together | Every electron starts drifting at once | Not one electron travelling |
| Charge already in wire | Electrons fill the whole circuit | Current is a chain reaction |

**Current — the two pictures classified**

| Picture | Quantity | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| Microscopic | Drift velocity | I = nAev |
| Macroscopic | Current | Charge per second |
| Speed note | Drift is mm/s | Signal travels near light speed |

subtopics.name: Current
points: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t
Conventional current flows opposite to electron flow

subtopics.name: Drift velocity
points: Electrons drift slowly in the direction opposite the field, superimposed on random thermal motion
Typical drift speed is about 10^-4 m/s, far slower than the signal speed
The electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights instantly

subtopics.name: I = nAev_d
points: n is free electron density, A cross-sectional area, e electronic charge, v_d drift velocity
Current depends on drift velocity, not on the random thermal speed
Larger area or higher electron density gives more current for the same drift speed

subtopics.name: Why drift is slow
points: Electrons collide constantly with the lattice and lose directed momentum
The drift velocity is the small average velocity superimposed on thermal motion
Increasing temperature increases collisions and reduces drift velocity, raising resistivity

subtopics.name: Current density and mobility
points: J = I/A = n e v_d, a vector quantity
Mobility mu = v_d/E measures how easily carriers move

subtopics.name: Numerical anchors
points: For copper, n is about 8.5 x 10^28 per cubic metre
